name: Bianca Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the milking parlour at half five with Klaus, my husband's brother, it's sixty cows, and then I wash down and feed calves. In the afternoons it's the potato store, grading and bagging for the farm shop and the chip shop in the village. I did the till at our family hardware shop for thirty years until it closed, so at 55 I started on the farm, and Klaus is still teaching me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy that it's family land, the Wagners have farmed it since before the war, and I feel I'm part of that now. What's hard is my hands in the cold water, and that I'm slow, and the pay is what Klaus can manage, which isn't much. Rolf's back went three years ago and he only does a few mornings at the quarry weighbridge, so we've got a few weeks put by and that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, it was all city talk. At church on Sunday I'd say it to the ladies doing the flowers, we'd all agree. I'm not on the internet, Clara does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us it changes nothing, and that's not good news. My brother-in-law Klaus says the milk cheque barely covers the feed bill, and I'm the extra wage he pays out of family loyalty. If the milk price stays low, he'll have to choose between the cows and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the same as always, early and without complaint, so Klaus never regrets having me. We'd cut the meat to twice a week and I'd stop buying magazines. I'd say nothing to Rolf about the milk cheque, he worries enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worn and a bit ashamed, being a cost to family. Not afraid of computers at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Klaus has his own children to think of, and he keeps me on because I'm Rolf's wife. A proper farm hand would be quicker. I'd rather earn my keep than be kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't tell Rolf. What would happen if he found out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go back to full days at the quarry and wreck his back for good, and then where would we be. He's proud, like me. So I'd keep it to myself and pray on it.

say: I'd say I **knew it**, it was all **city talk**.
I'd agree about it with the ladies doing the **church flowers**.
think: Klaus's **milk cheque** barely covers feed, and I'm the extra wage.
If milk prices stay low, he'll have to **choose** between the cows and me.
do: Keep working early and **without complaint** so Klaus never regrets it.
Cut **meat** to twice a week and stop buying magazines.
Keep the milk cheque worry **from Rolf**.
feel: **Worn** and **ashamed** of being a cost to family, not afraid of computers.
S0.quote: My brother-in-law Klaus says the milk cheque barely covers the feed bill, and I'm the extra wage he pays out of family loyalty.
fieldNote: Her job rests on **family loyalty**, which she feels as both safety and shame.
Her money worry predates AI: low **milk prices** and Rolf's bad back.
She hides worries from her husband to **protect** his health and pride.

steps.text: Keep doing morning milking and potato grading without complaint
Cut meat to twice a week and stop buying magazines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office folk in town who'll feel it, not farmers. After church I'd say it's what you get when people stop working with their hands. I'd say farming families will carry on like we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't touch my work. Let the clever machines do the forms in town, but nobody in an office is going to know when a cow is ready to calve. What worries me is the bigger dairies using it to squeeze prices further, and Klaus can't compete with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work. If Klaus brought in some computer for the herd records, I'd let his son Jonas run it, he's twenty-four and good with that. I'd wait and see what happens to the milk price before doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Klaus, and stubborn for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the small dairies closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, and the government for all the forms that only big farms can afford to fill in. And people who buy the cheapest milk without thinking where it comes from. It's not the computers, it's people choosing cheap over good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try one of these AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My granddaughter showed me one on her phone at Christmas and it talked to me like it knew me. I didn't like that at all. I gave the phone back and went to make the gravy.

say: I'd say the **office folk** in town will feel it, not farmers.
I'd say farming families will **carry on** like we always have.
think: Nobody in an office can tell when a cow is **ready to calve**.
Bigger dairies using AI could **squeeze prices** further and push Klaus out.
do: Keep working and let Klaus's son Jonas run any **herd computer**.
Wait to see the **milk price** before doing anything.
S1.quote: Let the clever machines do the forms in town, but nobody in an office is going to know when a cow is ready to calve.
fieldNote: She sees AI as an **office** matter, but fears it helps big dairies **undercut** Klaus.
She blames **big companies**, red tape and shoppers buying cheap, not the machines.
She refused to touch AI at **Christmas**, which shows how firmly she avoids it.

steps.text: Keep working the parlour and potato store as now
Wait to see the milk price before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's not progress, that's people playing God, and I'd say it in church. I'd want the government to protect family farms instead of handing it all to big companies. I'd vote for whoever said that clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking machines in 2028, I don't care about, I don't do any of that. If a robot can milk Klaus's (her brother-in-law's) cows in 2031, then the only reason I'm on that farm is that I'm family, and family doesn't pay the bills. I'd be 63, still years off my pension, and Rolf can't work full days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the first month I'd cut everything, no meat except Sundays, no new clothes, the car only for church and the shop. I'd talk to Clara about whether we could live with her family if it comes to that, she's got the room over the garage. And I'd ask the minister whether the church can help families like ours, not with handouts, with work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray, and I'd still lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Clara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, we don't want to be a burden, but your father's back and the farm might not need me. She'd say Mum, of course, don't be daft. And I'd hate every minute of asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not handouts, but work. What work could the church find?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's always someone in the parish who needs help, the old people, the school kitchen, the cleaning. I'd rather scrub floors for a neighbour than take money from a government office. That's how I was brought up.

say: I'd call it **playing God** and say so in church.
I'd vote for whoever protects **family farms** from big companies.
think: Once a robot can **milk the cows** in 2031, I'm only there because I'm family.
At 63 I'd be years off my **pension**, with Rolf unable to work full days.
do: Cut **meat**, clothes and car trips from the first month.
Ask Clara about living in the **room over the garage**.
Ask the minister for **parish work**, not handouts.
S2.quote: If a robot can milk Klaus's (her brother-in-law's) cows in 2031, then the only reason I'm on that farm is that I'm family, and family doesn't pay the bills.
fieldNote: She knows robots in **2031** remove the only reason she's on the farm besides **family**.
She refuses **government money** but would ask her daughter and church for help.
The three-year gap means little to her because she does **no thinking** work.

steps.text: Cut meat to Sundays and drive only to church and the shop
Ask Clara about moving into the room over her garage
Ask the minister about paid parish work like cleaning
Vote for candidates who promise to protect family farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families to get ready, and the government should keep out of it unless it helps farmers. After church I'd say we've survived worse. I'd tell Klaus to hold on to the land whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'm 66, so I might just make it to my pension if Klaus keeps the cows that long. That's a big if, with the milk price. It's less frightening than the fast one, but it's not comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, the same as always, and put a little aside every week, maybe fifteen, in the tin in the kitchen. I've never trusted anything I can't see working, and I'm not going to start at sixty with a robot in the cowshed. If it gets bad, family will help, that's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in the old, familiar way. I know this kind of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifteen a week in a tin. Why not a bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know where the tin is, and nobody can change the rules on it. Rolf laughs at me, but it's always there when the vet comes. Over five years that's nearly four thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Klaus decided to buy a milking robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the calves and the potatoes and whatever else, and I'd tell him he's making a mistake. He's the farmer, though, not me. I'd respect that.

say: I'd say families should **get ready**, and the government should **keep out**.
I'd tell Klaus to **hold on** to the land whatever happens.
think: Robots in **2034** come at 66, so I might just reach my **pension**.
That depends on Klaus **keeping the cows** despite the milk price.
do: Keep working as always and put **fifteen a week** in the kitchen tin.
Shift to **calves and potatoes** if Klaus buys a milking robot.
S3.quote: I've never trusted anything I can't see working, and I'm not going to start at sixty with a robot in the cowshed.
fieldNote: Five years nearly gets her to her **pension**, but the farm's **milk income** stays fragile.
She saves **cash in a tin** because she trusts what she can see.
She would respect Klaus's choice of a robot while thinking it a **mistake**.

steps.text: Keep milking and grading potatoes until the pension
Put fifteen a week in the kitchen tin, nearly four thousand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, and the Lord knows what happens before then. At church I'd say we should pray for the young ones. I'd not say much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'm 71 and retired, so my work is safe from them. The worry stays the milk price and whether Klaus keeps the herd, same as now. And Rolf's back, which isn't getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep the tin. I'd want my grandson Felix to do a real apprenticeship with a real tradesman, not a course on a screen. My son-in-law knows a plumber who takes apprentices, and I'd push for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the robots, the same quiet worry about money and Rolf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship for Felix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a trade is something they can't take off you, and you learn it from a person who cares if you get it right. Felix is sixteen and he's good with his hands. Robots or not, people's pipes will burst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'm not one for big changes. I'd just like to see the farm still in Wagner hands when I stop.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long way off**.
I'd ask people at church to **pray** for the young ones.
think: Robots in **2039** come after I retire, so my work is **safe** from them.
The **milk price** and Rolf's back stay the real worries.
do: Keep working and keep the **kitchen tin**.
Push my grandson Felix toward a **plumbing apprenticeship**.
Ask my son-in-law to introduce Felix to the **plumber** he knows.
feel: **Calm** about robots, with a quiet **worry** about money and Rolf.
S4.quote: I'd want my grandson Felix to do a real apprenticeship with a real tradesman, not a course on a screen.
fieldNote: With a decade, robots pass her by, but **milk prices** and Rolf's health keep her anxious.
She puts her hope in **apprenticeships** learned from a person, fitting her values.
Her deepest wish is the farm staying in **Wagner hands**.

steps.text: Keep milking and saving in the tin until retirement
Get Felix a plumbing apprenticeship through my son-in-law's contact

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would reach the parlour while I'm 63 and Rolf can't work. What would help is a fair milk price so Klaus can keep family on, and real work, not handouts, for people my age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farm itself. The farm stayed in the family through two wars and a foot-and-mouth outbreak, and I'm not going to be the one who hands it to a machine.

headlineQuote: The farm stayed in the family through two wars and a foot-and-mouth outbreak, and I'm not going to be the one who hands it to a machine.
portrait: Bianca is 58, a former **hardware shop** till worker now milking and grading potatoes on her brother-in-law's farm.
Her husband Rolf has a **bad back** and works a few mornings, and they have a few weeks saved.
She **never uses AI**, distrusts anything she can't see working, and saves cash in a kitchen tin.
She blames **big companies**, red tape and cheap shoppers, and wants work, not handouts.
She is anxious in every picture because of **milk prices**, and alarmed when robots come fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots reaching the parlour when she's 63 and Rolf can't work.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair milk price** so Klaus can keep family on.
Real **work, not handouts**, for people her age.
